Memristors, capable of varying resistance based on applied voltage, are a key component in neuromorphic computing and AI hardware accelerators due to their potential for high-density and low-power computing. However, the reliability of memristors is a major concern, particularly in applications where devices are used individually, rather than in parallel. This study investigates the reliability of memristor arrays by analyzing device-to-device variations and temporal fluctuations. A comprehensive model is developed to predict the reliability of memristor arrays under different conditions, including thermal effects. This model is then applied to a case study of a 102T1K memristor-based crossbar array used for binary classification tasks. The results show that the model is effective in predicting classification accuracy across a wide range of memristor variations and fluctuations. Notably, the study found that the accuracy of the memristor array is more susceptible to variations in the initial resistance distribution of individual memristors, rather than the distribution of their conductance windows. This finding has important implications for the design of reliable memristor-based hardware accelerators. A key takeaway from this study is that the reliability of memristor arrays is more closely tied to the initial resistance distribution of individual memristors, rather than the distribution of their conductance windows. This has significant implications for the design of reliable memristor-based hardware accelerators. Multimodal lecture videos, offering a combination of speaker visuals and presentation slides, are widely used in educational settings. They facilitate the transfer of knowledge and serve as a valuable resource for students. However, their content is often scattered, making it essential to develop an automatic method for creating a unified presentation. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that generates a synchronized video from a multimodal lecture. Our method utilizes a text-based model to create a unified presentation and a video editing technique to produce the final output. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through qualitative results, comparing it to existing approaches on YouTube videos. Additionally, we provide a user survey to validate the quality of our output. The associated code is available at \url{https://github.com/IBM/LectureMerging}. Experimental results show that our method outperforms existing approaches in creating a unified presentation. Furthermore, user feedback indicates a high level of satisfaction with the quality of our output. Our work has the potential to contribute to the development of future multimodal lecture analysis systems. Pre-trained models and the demo are accessible at \url{https://ibm.github.io/lecture-merging}. A video showcasing the results can be found at \url{https://youtu.be/6kQ6Q6Q6Q6Q}. We have conducted a comprehensive study of the magnetic Raman scattering in a two-dimensional antiferromagnet with a unique spin structure, using a theoretical model that incorporates both conventional and unconventional magnetic interactions. Our findings reveal distinct characteristics of the conventional and unconventional scattering processes, allowing us to identify the presence of a Haldane state in a real-world material. Specifically, we investigated the SrMnBi2 compound, a material known to host a Haldane state, and observed a significant suppression of the conventional magnetic scattering at low energies, consistent with theoretical predictions. This study provides a new approach for understanding the properties of Haldane states in two-dimensional antiferromagnets. Additionally, our results offer a valuable tool for exploring the relationship between spin correlations and lattice distortions in these materials, and for investigating the effects of spin-orbit coupling on their magnetic properties. Finally, our work paves the way for the application of magnetic Raman scattering as a diagnostic tool for identifying Haldane states in two-dimensional antiferromagnets. The concept of metaphorical abstraction is crucial in conveying imaginative ideas, yet it remains a complex and understudied area in research, despite its potential to facilitate generative thinking across various domains. This study delves into the role of metaphorical abstraction in enhancing human-AI collaboration in creating new concepts. To investigate this, we developed a novel dataset consisting of metaphorically abstract sentences, paired with literal translations, and explored the potential of using these literal translations as a starting point for generating more abstract descriptions. Our findings indicate that using metaphorical abstraction significantly enhances the quality of novel ideas produced by AI systems, particularly when employing a dataset-driven approach. Furthermore, we discovered that incorporating the human evaluator's past responses can lead to more accurate and creative outcomes. To facilitate further research, we have made our dataset and pre-trained models publicly available. Ultimately, our research highlights the potential of metaphorical abstraction as a powerful tool for collaborative idea generation. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/ntu-cllab/metab.git. Additional resources are available at https://ntu-cllab.github.io/metab/ and can be contacted via [xushengyu@ntu.edu.sg](mailto:xushengyu@ntu.edu.sg). The authors are also part of the NLP Lab at Nanyang Technological University. Supplemental information is provided in the appendices. 
Keywords: metaphorical abstraction, collaborative idea generation, human-AI interaction, dataset-driven models, back-translation, response-based models.

By leveraging a trainable attention mechanism, our A-Net model can adapt to a wide range of intensity variations, making it more effective for medical image segmentation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our A-Net model outperforms the original UNet model, particularly in scenarios with significant intensity variations, resulting in improved segmentation accuracy. Additionally, our A-Net model can be efficiently trained using a single GPU, making it a more viable option for real-world applications. As a result, attackers cannot effectively employ conventional OFDM demodulation techniques, thereby significantly increasing the difficulty of hacking the system. The results demonstrate that Rand-OFDM offers greater security benefits compared to conventional OFDM, particularly in jamming scenarios, where Rand-OFDM's performance remains nearly unaffected, whereas OFDM's performance degrades significantly. Furthermore, Rand-OFDM's performance is shown to be robust against jamming when the jamming power is high, whereas OFDM's performance is severely impaired. The proposed system also exhibits good performance in terms of signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio, comparable to conventional OFDM, when the jamming power is low. preserves their overall behavior. We're particularly interested in understanding how
these systems behave when their connections form a tree-like structure. Our key
finding shows that such networks can be broken down into simpler components, even
when the individual automata are complex and can produce an infinite sequence of
actions. This result has far-reaching implications, allowing us to solve several
problems related to infinite-state system analysis. Specifically, we've developed
a method to determine whether such networks will always reach a stable state and
also identified the minimum number of automata required to achieve this state. 
Furthermore, our approach can be adapted to analyze systems with more general
network topologies, although this would lead to less accurate estimates of their
behavior. Our work is also applicable to more complex systems involving multiple
automata and transitions that depend on the collective actions of these components. 
Additionally, our approach has been successfully implemented in a tool called
DynaMo, which has been used to verify safety properties in a real-world system. 
This tool has successfully identified potential security risks in a system used to
control the flow of traffic in a specific region of the UK.

To fully comprehend documents, it's crucial to be able to identify and interpret the various graphical components present, including tables, figures, and their respective captions. To achieve this, we propose a novel end-to-end framework that can simultaneously identify and classify a wide range of graphical elements and their captions. Our framework leverages a unique graphical representation method that combines both the visual layout and the text content, allowing us to develop a robust pipeline for extracting graphical elements from complex documents. By incorporating a novel attention mechanism, we can effectively isolate and extract the graphical components, while also utilizing a conditional model to accurately identify the captions associated with each component. Our framework is evaluated on a large-scale dataset of 1,500 PDF files and demonstrates exceptional performance in both graphical component recognition and caption extraction. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applications of our framework by using the extracted graphical components to significantly enhance the accuracy of information extraction tasks. Our research is the first to address the challenging task of automatically identifying and extracting graphical components from complex documents. We introduce a new approach called SoftDICE, an advanced imitation learning technique that surpasses the previous method ValueDICE in terms of efficiency. In addition, we enhance SoftDICE by incorporating a new entropy regularization term that promotes more diverse and efficient exploration of the state space. Theoretical analysis confirms the improved efficiency of SoftDICE, and experimental results demonstrate its superiority over ValueDICE and other state-of-the-art imitation learning methods in various continuous control tasks. GPP outperforms existing pruning methods in terms of accuracy and out-of-distribution performance on various models and datasets, achieving up to 60% fewer parameters without a decrease in accuracy. GPP achieves this by analyzing gradient patterns in different layers and pruning them based on their relevance to the model's decision-making process. We've also introduced a new pruning criterion, the Gradient Pattern Pattern Similarity (GPPS), which measures the similarity between layers' gradient patterns and their impact on the model's decision-making. GPP uses GPPS to prune layers based on their relevance to the model's decision-making process, resulting in more accurate and efficient pruning. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of GPP in pruning models without a full model, a significant improvement over existing pruning methods. Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success across various fields, 
but their vulnerability to subtle manipulations has raised significant concerns. 
To address this issue, researchers have developed a robust adversarial training approach, 
which involves training models against anticipated attacks. However, this technique comes at a cost. 
Adversarial training methods often lead to overfitting and may not effectively counter all types of attacks. 
In response, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a self-supervised learning framework to enhance a deep neural network's resilience to adversarial attacks. This approach involves a self-supervised discriminator that is trained to identify and eliminate noise in the input data. This process is seamlessly integrated into the adversarial training process, 
which not only enhances the robustness of the model but also minimizes the risk of overfitting. 
Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing adversarial training methods on CIFAR-10 data. Furthermore, it offers a unique advantage by allowing the model to learn from its mistakes and improve its ability to recognize adversarial samples. 
Our findings also indicate that this approach can be adapted to improve the robustness of pre-trained models.

We investigate the lattice models of conformal field theory on a torus, 
focusing on the crossing equation and its solutions. 
We demonstrate that the crossing multipliers of these models are linked to the characters of the conformal field theory and prove the validity of the crossing equation in this context. 
We also show that the crossing multipliers satisfy a specific mathematical relationship known as the 5j relation. 
Furthermore, we examine the crossing multipliers of the lattice Ising, Potts, and eight-vertex models, 
and derive their exact values for finite lattices, 
which are consistent with the predictions of conformal field theory in the thermodynamic limit. 
This work provides a foundation for further research on crossing equations in lattice models and offers a new approach to conformal field theory. 
Additionally, we discuss the potential applications of this research to the context of the AdS/BCFT correspondence. 
We also explore the implications of our findings for the lattice models of conformal field theory in relation to the conformal bootstrap program. 
Finally, we suggest that the crossing multipliers of these models may be used to determine the central charge of the conformal field theory.

A generative adversarial network (GAN) generates data samples by competing between a generator and a discriminator. However, during training, GANs often experience mode collapse, where the generator produces limited variations of the data. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach that utilizes a mode coverage loss function. This method involves creating a binary mask for the input data, followed by a generator that produces a masked version of the data. The discriminator then evaluates the masked data, enabling it to identify and classify the hidden parts of the input. By incorporating a mode coverage loss, this approach encourages the generator to produce a diverse range of data. Experimentation demonstrates that our method effectively minimizes mode collapse in GANs. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be adapted to various GAN architectures and successfully improves the quality of generated data in applications such as image and video generation. This research introduces a groundbreaking approach for identifying individuals walking using spiking neural networks with adaptive synapses. Our method leverages a unique combination of a Sallen-Key filter to capture temporal patterns and a spiking network to extract frequency-based features. These features are then transmitted to a two-layer network, where they are filtered through experience-based synaptic adjustments. As a result, the network becomes highly responsive to walking patterns while largely ignoring other types of movement. Our experiment demonstrates that this innovative system surpasses existing methods in a variety of challenging environments, including varying speeds, different walking surfaces, and distracting objects. Additionally, the network's ability to learn from experience enables it to maintain a high level of performance over an extended period without requiring additional training. This study's findings hold significant implications for the development of wearable devices that can accurately track human movement. The Mixture of Experts (MoE) model is a powerful tool for resolving the vanishing gradient problem in deep learning. It achieves this by dividing the network into multiple sub-networks, each trained separately. However, this approach can be inefficient due to the need for frequent expert network updates during training. To address this issue, we introduce a novel method called Gating Dropout, which enables the utilization of under-trained expert networks during training. By randomly disabling the gating network during training, we can update the model using previously trained expert networks. This approach not only accelerates the training process but also reduces the computational cost associated with expert training. Our experimental results demonstrate that Gating Dropout can significantly enhance the performance of MoE models, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods in various tasks, including language modeling and image classification. Link prediction in knowledge graphs is a critical issue that has garnered significant attention from researchers. Current approaches face two primary problems: (1) they fail to adequately capture the complex semantic relationships between entities and their associated attributes, and (2) they are unable to effectively transfer knowledge from one knowledge graph to another. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework called Graph2Graph, which combines a graph-to-graph model with a knowledge graph embedding approach. Our approach first utilizes a graph-to-graph model to identify the underlying relationships between entities across different knowledge graphs, and then generates a new knowledge graph that encodes the common semantic relationships between entities. Next, we employ a knowledge graph embedding method to learn the embeddings of entities from both the original and generated graphs. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed Graph2Graph model. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhongjianjing/Graph2Graph. Additionally, we have made our pre-trained models and evaluation datasets accessible at https://huggingface.co/Graph2Graph. This novel term is derived from the integration of the 10-dimensional Chern-Simons 3-form, resulting from the condensation of the 6-dimensional fields from the original 10-dimensional action. Consequently, the reduced low-energy action is found to be consistent with the Einstein-Cartan-Yang-Mills-Dirac action, which is a well-known theory in the 2+4 dimensional space. Our approach involves utilizing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to estimate GMM parameters and, subsequently, to simulate returns. This method is then applied to the S&P 500 index, enabling the derivation of VaR estimates for a portfolio consisting of multiple assets. Furthermore, we found that GMMs can accurately predict the likelihood of returns falling within specific quantile ranges. This method also enables the calculation of conditional VaR, which is essential for managing portfolio risk. Our approach is particularly beneficial in situations where returns exhibit fat tails and non-normal distributions. Finally, we highlight the potential for further research in this area. Paired conditional random fields (CRFs) are commonly employed in sequence
labeling tasks, such as part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition.
However, their training process is often hindered by the computational expense
of mean-field inference, which grows exponentially with the data size. To
overcome this limitation, we propose a novel, attention-based approach to
approximate mean-field inference, which leverages a graph attention network to
compute marginal probabilities. Our proposed method, dubbed P-GAT, outperforms
traditional mean-field inference methods, achieving a 2.5-fold training speedup
on the CoNLL-2003 English data set. Moreover, P-GAT yields superior results
compared to existing state-of-the-art models, demonstrating its efficacy. To
further enhance the applicability of paired CRFs, we introduce a novel model
that integrates a graph attention network with a mean-field inference algorithm,
which can be combined with any existing mean-field model. Our proposed method,
which we call the mean-field attention network, achieves state-of-the-art
results on the CoNLL-2003 English data set, surpassing previous models by a
notable margin. Our findings suggest that mean-field attention can be a viable
alternative to more complex attention-based models, offering a more
efficient approach to modeling long-range dependencies. The code and models used
in this research are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyu-lyj/P-GAT.

distinctive technique, dubbed "dark-knowledge," to enhance the removal of haze
from images. The proposed framework employs a unique combination of a haze-inducing
network and a haze-reversing network, which are trained jointly in an adversarial
manner. The haze-inducing network generates images with varying levels of haze,
while the haze-reversing network aims to identify and eliminate the artificial
haze produced by the first network. The integration of these two networks relies
on a sophisticated loss function that incorporates a novel "dark-knowledge"
component, which is designed to promote the production of realistic, natural
images. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework surpasses the current
state-of-the-art methods in both subjective and objective evaluations. The code
implementing our framework is available for download at https://github.com/zhw2509/Dark-Knowledge.

This paper introduces an active learning approach for selecting the most informative samples to include in the training dataset for deep convolutional neural networks. By leveraging this strategy, we aim to enhance the performance of visual tracking tasks. The proposed method, called Active Learning for Visual Tracking (ALFT), is a two-stage process that first identifies the most valuable training samples and then uses these samples to train a high-performing tracking model. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the OTB50 and LaSOT datasets demonstrate that ALFT surpasses state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin, with results showing a notable improvement of 7.6% and 9.1% in success rates and frame-wise accuracy, respectively. Additionally, ALFT exhibits exceptional robustness against challenging scenarios such as rapid motion, occlusion, and similar-looking objects. This paper details the development of a Tatar language corpus named TatCorpus 1.0, specifically designed for the Tatar language, which is spoken by over one and a half million people, primarily in Tatarstan and neighboring regions. Currently, there is a lack of standardized linguistic resources for the Tatar language, making it challenging for researchers to work with. To address this issue, we have compiled a comprehensive Tatar language corpus, comprising 30,000 sentences, and created 10,000 additional sentences through crowdsourcing to enhance the reliability of part-of-speech tagging. Furthermore, we have designed a part-of-speech tagset and manually annotated the corpus using a set of commonly used Tatar words. The results of an automatic part-of-speech tagging system trained on our corpus are also presented and compared to those obtained from a manually tagged test set. The developed resources are expected to facilitate linguistic research and teaching of the Tatar language, particularly in machine learning and natural language processing. Additionally, we have made our resources available to the academic community, and our approach can be applied to other under-represented languages. The Tatar language corpus, along with the accompanying code, is accessible online at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/ArtemSorokin/TatCorpus. 

Keywords: Tatar language, machine learning, natural language processing, corpus linguistics, linguistic resources, part-of-speech tagging.

pruning techniques. By leveraging the concept of sparsity of the weight
intermediates during training, Structured Pruning generates a compact neural
network by removing zero-weight connections in a single training cycle. The method
incorporates a weight masking mechanism that limits the propagation of zero-weight
connections, thereby ensuring the model's performance integrity. We demonstrate
the efficacy of Structured Pruning by achieving comparable results to state-of-the-art
pruning methods on ImageNet using a ResNet-50 model, with the added benefit of
reduced computational costs. The accompanying code can be found on the GitHub
repository located at https://github.com/IBM/structured-pruning. Structured Pruning
is poised to facilitate the development of more efficient neural networks for
resource-constrained edge devices. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/IBM/structured-pruning.

We introduce ParaNet, a novel 3D point cloud representation that eschews conventional multi-view projection and voxelization methods in favor of a more direct approach. By projecting 3D points onto a 2D grid and selecting only the nearest neighbor to each cell, ParaNet enables a highly efficient and adaptive encoding of 3D data. This approach allows for the creation of a compact, per-cell vector that effectively captures local geometric information. By aggregating these local encodings, ParaNet achieves a global representation of the 3D point cloud. Through extensive experimentation, ParaNet has demonstrated its ability to match or surpass state-of-the-art performance on a range of 3D point cloud tasks, including classification, segmentation, and classification with occlusion. Notably, ParaNet achieves a 3x reduction in memory usage and a 3x increase in training speed compared to the most competitive baseline. This significant improvement in efficiency is expected to facilitate the wider adoption of 3D point cloud models in real-world applications. ParaNet code is available at https://github.com/taosenchuan/Paranet. Furthermore, ParaNet has achieved top results on the Waymo Open Perception Challenge 2022, ranking first in the segmentation and classification with occlusion tasks. Our approach is adaptable to different fairness objectives and can be applied to various neural networks, with initial results demonstrating its potential to achieve fairness with minimal computational overhead. Our research marks the first to integrate fairness into federated learning, with significant implications for applications like medical imaging and autonomous driving. transcription. Our proposed approach utilizes a pre-trained speech 
model and a text encoder, which are jointly fine-tuned on raw speech 
from various languages. Experimental results demonstrate that this 
method successfully enables cross-lingual speech recognition in 7 
languages with minimal transcribed data available. Furthermore, our 
approach outperforms existing methods in 6 out of 7 test languages,

This method, which is based on the principle of curriculum learning, identifies and prioritizes samples with the highest potential for improvement. By doing so, it enables the model to learn more effectively from a larger dataset. Our results show that Curriculum Pseudo Labeling outperforms existing methods on a range of benchmark datasets, achieving a notable improvement of 0.7% in accuracy on the CIFAR-100 dataset. Additionally, it demonstrates exceptional robustness against model overfitting, requiring significantly fewer labeled examples for training. For instance, it achieves the same accuracy as 86.1% using only 80% of the labeled data required by the baseline method. This paper introduces a novel image classification and saliency detection model, 
utilizing the p-Laplacian operator to extract the most representative features 
from input images. By employing the p-Laplacian operator, the proposed model aims 
to minimize the influence of local image details, thereby enhancing the 
saliency map's global quality. A novel loss function is also presented to 
evaluate the saliency map's overall quality. Experimental results demonstrate 
the superior performance of the proposed method in comparison to existing 
approaches. Furthermore, the proposed model's computational efficiency is 
demonstrated through its ability to process images at a faster rate than its 
conventional counterparts. The project's code is publicly available on GitHub 
at https://github.com/abdolnabi/P-Laplacian-Image-Saliency-Detection. 
Additionally, the project's website can be accessed at http://nai-lab.org/plassd. 
The project's dataset and model are also available for download from the 
Microsoft Azure repository.

This paper introduces the It\^oWave vocoder, a novel approach that utilizes a stochastic differential equation to generate voice waveforms. The It\^oWave model is based on a Wiener process that is influenced by a specific set of parameters, which are determined through the analysis of speech patterns. This novel vocoder is capable of producing high-quality voice replicas that are comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while also offering a unique advantage in terms of its ability to generate speech under uncertain conditions. Furthermore, the It\^oWave model provides a new perspective on the underlying mechanisms of voice production and may potentially lead to the development of more efficient vocoders in the future. To support the validity of these findings, a comprehensive experimental study has been conducted, which includes both objective and subjective evaluations of the It\^oWave vocoder's performance. The accompanying code and data are publicly available for further research and analysis. These metrics, derived from the ambient space's metric, possess properties that facilitate the construction of a Riemannian submersion with a complex structure-compatible with the adapted metric. Consequently, the resulting quotient space is equipped with a Hermitian symmetric space structure. Additionally, we provide examples of such symmetric pairs and Hermitian symmetric spaces, including those not previously documented. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the adapted metric on a Hermitian symmetric space and the restriction of the ambient space's metric to its isometric group of holomorphic transformations. Finally, we outline a general strategy for constructing Hermitian symmetric spaces from the quotient of a symmetric Riemannian manifold by its compact connected component, provided that the resulting quotient space is Kähler. A gradient iterative approach for solving symmetric generalized eigenvalue problems is presented, where the gradient is calculated using a preconditioned finite difference. This method is flexible and accommodates a broad class of norms, enabling the selection of a norm that aligns with the expected properties of the extreme eigenvalues. Convergence rates are established for the gradient iterative method under standard assumptions, demonstrating its reliability. Building upon this foundation, we develop a non-monotone variant of the gradient iterative method and investigate its convergence. Notably, under certain conditions, this variant is proven to converge linearly, and its performance is evaluated using a block Krylov solver. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, showcasing their ability to efficiently locate interior or exterior eigenpairs in a reasonable number of iterations. This research is a continuation of an earlier study, which can be found in reference [21]. The associated code is publicly available in the repository [35]. The findings of this paper are also applicable to the solution of symmetric saddle-point systems, which can be viewed as a special case of the generalized eigenvalue problem. The presented results are therefore relevant to the development of iterative methods for these systems. An extension of the gradient iterative method to the case of non-symmetric generalized eigenvalue problems is also explored. Collaborative filtering models have achieved significant success in personalized
recommendations by leveraging user-item interactions, but they are susceptible to
popularity bias, which skews recommendations towards well-known items, ultimately
leading to recommendations lacking accuracy. To address this issue, we introduce
a new approach that incorporates a debiasing layer to remove the popularity bias
from collaborative filtering models. By modeling user-item interactions as a
combination of a biased signal and an unbiased signal, our method utilizes a
pre-trained model to extract these signals. The unbiased signal serves as a
reliable indicator of item quality, which is essential for accurate recommendations
in collaborative filtering models. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to
any collaborative filtering model, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by
integrating it into several prominent models, including NeuMF and NeuMF-VAE. The
results of our experiments on various datasets demonstrate that our method
significantly improves recommendation accuracy, particularly in scenarios with
popularity bias. Additionally, our method outperforms existing debiasing techniques
and achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets. The code
implementing our method is available for public use. For further information, please
visit our project website at https://github.com/THU-TCM/debiasingCF.

We establish Galois coverings on tropical curves that satisfy a Galois correspondence and a spectral correspondence analogous to their algebraic counterparts. This framework allows us to define and interpret positive-dimensional Galois coverings of tropical curves. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every finite Galois covering of a tropical curve as a quotient of the affine line is necessarily representable by a rational graph. Additionally, we show that every finite Galois covering of the affine line as a tropical curve corresponds to a graph with a single edge. This result is complemented by the observation that every finite Galois covering of the affine line as a tropical curve is either non-degenerate or corresponds to a graph with a self-loop. Lastly, we provide a Galois correspondence for the preimage of a tropical curve's skeleton under a finite Galois covering. In classification tasks, especially with scarce training data, transfer learning is a widely used technique that draws on knowledge from related, yet distinct, datasets. A key challenge lies in identifying the optimal level of information transfer. A new approach addresses this issue by treating the selection of transfer data as a search problem within the original dataset. By applying a novel metric that captures the similarity between datasets, the method can identify the most relevant data for transfer learning. A proposed algorithm leverages this metric to efficiently find suitable data for enhancing classification performance. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this approach over current methods in various domains, including text classification and image recognition. Furthermore, the method can be adapted for multiple related datasets and is not limited to a single source dataset. A notable advantage is its ability to handle datasets of vastly different sizes, a limitation of some existing transfer learning methods. We demonstrate that the directional asymptotic cone of an infinite, countable group is inherently decomposable into distinct, non-intersecting subsets, each corresponding to a specific group element's orbit within its asymptotic cone. This finding contradicts a long-held assumption in the field, previously suggesting a connection between cone separability and the group being either finite or unbounded in growth. Notably, we provide a concrete example of a countable group that exhibits cone separability yet lacks any non-trivial unbounded expansion. Our proof relies on a novel asymptotic cone characterization for groups exhibiting non-trivial unbounded expansion. Additionally, we establish a similar separability property for the directional cone of a finite simple group, thereby resolving a previously posed question by A. Lucchini. This finding is further extended to include finite simple groups characterized by their unimodular property. Finally, we derive a characterization of the directional cone of a finite group, ultimately resolving a long-standing conjecture by A. Lucchini. This proof is facilitated by the application of a previously established result by A. Lucchini and G. Taback. Deep learning models have achieved impressive results in point cloud classification, 
but their effectiveness is limited by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality 
point cloud datasets. To address this issue, we have developed a novel data 
generation technique that produces realistic, labeled point clouds with 
arbitrary numbers of points. By leveraging a pre-trained generative adversarial 
network, we can efficiently create new datasets for various classification tasks. 
In our experiments, the generated data demonstrates exceptional similarity to 
actual datasets and exhibits a notable ability to enhance the performance of deep 
neural networks. Furthermore, the generated data exhibits a high degree of 
reusability, allowing it to improve model performance across multiple datasets. 
To facilitate the application of our method, we have created a new, large-scale 
dataset of indoor scenes, which we will make publicly available. The code for our 
method is also available online. The results of our experiments are available on 
Google Drive.

This project's design allows for the combination of various simulation packages, with the current setup featuring the SPHERE code for hadronic components and Geant4 for electromagnetic ones. A comprehensive review of the SPHERE code's advancements since its initial release is presented, accompanied by an in-depth examination of the results from recent CORSIKA 8 simulations, including comparisons with experimental data regarding particle production at air showers. Furthermore, the results from CORSIKA 8's interaction with multiple hadronic and cosmic ray simulation packages are discussed. This includes a discussion of the challenges encountered in simulating high-energy particles, such as those with energies above 100 TeV per nucleon. The current status of the SPHERE code is also outlined, along with prospects for its future development. This includes the potential implementation of a new, more advanced hadronic model, QGSII-B, which is expected to enhance the SPHERE code's capabilities for simulating high-energy particles. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) utilize temporal spikes to convey information,
similar to biological neural networks. SNNs have the potential to offer improved
energy efficiency and tolerance to hardware failures, making them suitable for
edge AI applications. However, the high computational costs associated with
simulating spiking events hinder the practical use of SNNs. To address this
issue, we have developed a new approach that combines the benefits of
approximation-based methods with the strengths of exact spiking event simulations.
Our proposed method, which integrates approximate and exact techniques, has been
applied to a range of SNNs, including both linear and non-linear models. The
results demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces the computational
overhead of SNN simulations while maintaining high accuracy. Furthermore, we have
extended our method to enable the efficient training of SNNs, and our
experiments have shown that it outperforms existing approximation-based methods
in terms of accuracy and energy efficiency. The source code for our method is
available online. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/IBM/Approx-SNN. 
A pre-trained model can be downloaded from https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13051. 
Please note that the code is intended for academic and research purposes only.

A novel spectral classification method has been developed to distinguish between stars, galaxies, and quasars based on their spectroscopic characteristics. This approach utilizes a deep neural network to identify these celestial objects from a comprehensive dataset comprising over 1.2 million spectra. The resulting classification model demonstrates exceptional performance in determining the correct object class for individual spectra, boasting a remarkable accuracy of 99.07%. Furthermore, the method's ability to identify galaxy-galaxy and star-star binary systems has been successfully demonstrated, with a notable accuracy rate of 99.46%. The application of traceability in software engineering has been well-documented, 
with numerous approaches proposed in literature. However, the majority of these 
methods rely on manual tracing, which is time-consuming and labor-intensive. 
To address this limitation, researchers have turned to the application of deep 
learning models in creating software traces. This study presents a novel approach 
to automatically generating trace models from requirements and source code. By 
utilizing a graph neural network, the proposed method is capable of identifying 
connections between requirements and source code elements. An evaluation of the 
approach was conducted using a dataset consisting of 30 projects, with results 
indicating a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method was found 
to outperform a baseline approach in terms of performance. Additionally, the 
approach was applied to a real-world project, with the generated trace model 
evaluated by a human expert. The findings suggest that the proposed method is 
capable of producing trace models that are both accurate and relevant. This 
study contributes to the development of a fully automated approach to 
automatically generating trace models in software engineering projects. The code 
implementing the proposed approach is publicly available on GitHub.

released under an open-source license.

Finally, we provide a simulation-based evaluation of our method using a multirobot system with non-linear dynamics. The results demonstrate the superiority of our method in providing accurate state estimates compared to other observers. Specifically, we found that the proposed observer achieved an average error of 0.0003, while the other observers had an average error of 0.0005. Furthermore, we outline potential research directions that can help bridge the gap between current chatbot capabilities and the creation of truly conversational AI systems. Ultimately, we aim to stimulate further research in this field by highlighting the importance of background-aware chatbots, and to encourage a shift towards more natural and engaging conversational AI experiences. Hyperspectral image denoising has been a significant focus in recent years, 
due to the high value of hyperspectral images in various applications.

high computational requirements and the need for extensive data augmentation.

integrates a denoising network with a self-supervised feature learning 
component, which utilizes a contrastive loss function to learn robust, 
semantically meaningful features from hyperspectral images.

extraction and improve the model's performance.

outperforming existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

complexity compared to the state-of-the-art method,

This paper introduces a novel approach for analyzing oscillatory signals by
integrating the frequency modulated Möbius (FMM) model with the time-frequency
reconstruction method. The FMM model is capable of representing complex
oscillatory patterns, and when combined with time-frequency reconstruction,
it enables the identification of time-varying frequencies. The proposed method
employs a combination of time-frequency atomic decomposition and the FMM model
to track the evolution of oscillatory signals. The effectiveness of this
approach is demonstrated through both simulated and real-world examples. The
simulated results confirm the method's ability to accurately reconstruct the
underlying signals and their frequencies over time. Furthermore, the method is
applied to analyze electroencephalogram (EEG) data from subjects performing a
visual oddball task, yielding promising outcomes. The proposed method is
compared to other time-frequency techniques, showcasing its advantages in
capturing the dynamics of oscillatory signals. The accompanying code for this
study is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmedblaha/FMM-TFR.

decomposition, Time-varying frequencies, Non-stationary oscillatory signals.

This research presents a novel approach to categorizing academic documents from open-access repositories by file extension, which is a frequently overlooked aspect of metadata. We also examined the geographical distribution of document types, highlighting regional variations and notable discrepancies between repository descriptions and their actual content. Furthermore, we identified a correlation between the repository descriptions and the prevailing document types. The findings from this study demonstrate that file extension classification can be a reliable method for document identification, and we propose its integration into repository metadata standards. Additionally, we recommend that repository descriptions accurately reflect the types of documents they contain. This paper explores the possibility of achieving simultaneous state estimation and output control for a system that is vulnerable to an eavesdropper's interception of sensor and control signals. To address this threat, we introduce a privacy-preserving approach utilizing homomorphic encryption for secure state data sharing, while also implementing encrypted control inputs sent via an unsecured channel. Our solution involves a two-stage process where the first stage involves developing a state estimator and controller based on a shared, encrypted state. Subsequently, in the second stage, we design a second estimator that utilizes the initial estimator's output along with the system's input-output data to estimate the system's state, thus achieving resilience to an eavesdropper's interception. Our proposed solution is demonstrated through a simulation-based study on a network of multiple agents. Additionally, we examine the trade-offs between state estimation accuracy, output regulation, and system security in the presence of an eavesdropper. Our results indicate that the proposed solution can achieve near-optimal state estimation accuracy, comparable output regulation performance, and a high level of robustness against an eavesdropper's interception of sensor and control signals. Our findings suggest that the proposed solution is a promising approach for ensuring the security of multi-agent systems in the presence of an eavesdropper. Finally, we discuss the limitations of our proposed solution and outline potential avenues for future research. The goal of open set recognition is to develop a classifier that accurately identifies known classes while distinguishing between known classes and unknown classes. This area of research has significant implications for applications like anomaly detection, where existing classifiers may produce false positive predictions for unknown data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach called the open set classifier, which combines a discriminatively trained classifier with a probabilistic model that estimates the distribution of the data. This model enables the classifier to differentiate between known and unknown data. We demonstrate that our proposed method can be viewed as a variant of the maximum entropy approach and provide a theoretical explanation for its effectiveness. Experimental results confirm that our approach surpasses existing methods in open set recognition tasks. Furthermore, we show that our method can be adapted to work with deep neural networks, which have the potential to be used as feature extractors. This allows for the application of our approach to various domains, including those where the training and test data are not available. We also present a new benchmark dataset for open set anomaly detection to facilitate further research in this area. To promote reproducibility, we release our code and models for public use. High-dimensional time series data often necessitates the use of vector autoregressive (VAR) models, but these can be problematic when the number of variables exceeds the number of observations. This issue is addressed by employing a kernel-based approach that reduces dimensionality by transforming the data into a compact representation. A novel, adaptive kernel approach is presented, where the transformation is tailored to the specific structure of the data, and a method for estimating the associated parameters is outlined. This technique is then applied to a VAR model, where the resulting transformed data is utilized to obtain accurate estimates of the model's parameters. This approach is particularly valuable in situations where the number of variables is large relative to the number of observations, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments. Furthermore, the practical application of this method is illustrated through an analysis of high-dimensional stock market data. This example reveals that the proposed method is capable of identifying complex patterns in the data that more traditional methods fail to uncover. Consequently, the resulting VAR model is more effective at predicting future returns. All relevant code is made available for public use. The findings of this research are expected to provide valuable insights for researchers working with high-dimensional time series data. An accompanying R package, called Rkvar, has been developed to facilitate the use of this method in practical applications. This package can be accessed through the Comprehensive R Archive Network at https://cran.rstudio.com/. Estimating the depth of light fields is a complex task, particularly when dealing with large datasets. A recent approach, Light Field Depth Estimation via Cost Volume, achieved good results but required significant resources. In contrast, our method offers an efficient and straightforward alternative, leveraging a pre-trained network to predict depth values from camera coordinates and color channels. By applying this approach, we were able of surpassing state-of-the-art performance while reducing computational complexity by over 90%. Additionally, our method excels in scenarios with low ray counts, a limitation of previous methods. To further enhance performance, we incorporated a novel technique that refines depth estimates through depth-aware super-resolution. The results demonstrate that our approach, which combines a simple cost constructor with a sophisticated refinement step, yields superior outcomes while being highly efficient.
